A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EPD disaggregation system and are readable throughout. V1 has 13 pages without appendices; v2 has 16 pages including Appendices A–D. Text, equations, tables, figures, and relocated material support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original GPU experiments measuring SLO attainment, first-token latency, memory capacity, and offline throughput across three multimodal models.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds NextQA evaluation, optimizer and role-switching ablations, and NPU experiments in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: V2 introduces dynamic role switching with explicit offload, migration, and onload steps for reallocating workers between stages. It also replaces v1's random-search configuration optimizer with Bayesian optimization. Asynchronous caching and intra-request parallelism were already present in v1.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic workloads only. V2 adds real video question-answering requests from NextQA and an online workload-shift scenario changing output demand from 50 to 500 tokens. The existing six- and eight-image synthetic scenarios remain in Appendix D.1.

E2.justification: DistServe and vLLM remain the external baselines. V2 removes the EPD-IRP comparator from the main SLO and TTFT plots, retaining a narrower comparison as 'w/o IRP' in Table 3. It adds controls without configuration optimization and without role switching in Tables 4–5.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce NextQA frame sampling, equal-eight-GPU configuration controls, a changing-output-length workload, and NPU-specific hardware, cache, and SLO settings. V2 also revises the stated TTFT endpoint from the decoder to the user and describes TPOT as inter-token latency excluding the first token. These reported definition changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds optimizer-versus-random-configuration and role-switching ablations, plus a GPU/NPU encoding-versus-prefill latency breakdown. Existing IRP evidence is narrowed from multi-model SLO and TTFT curves to a four-setting TTFT table. The offline resource-allocation and batch-size sensitivity analyses are retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Table 4 and Appendix B.4 newly estimate expected random-configuration performance using the sample mean of ten uniformly sampled configurations. This is configuration sampling, not ten repeated runs of one setting. Request-level TTFT boxplots remain; neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds NextQA and NPU outcomes and quantitative ablations. Table 4 reports goodput of 1.25 versus 0.56 requests/s for optimized versus averaged random configurations; Table 5 reports latency of 28.01 versus 61.10 seconds with versus without switching. Some retained InternVL2-8B baseline SLO curves also change. V1's memory Tables 2–4 retain their values as v2 Tables 1, 2, and 7.

T1.justification: The stage and migration equations, optimization objective, configuration variables, and GPU cost expression are retained. V2 mostly inlines or relocates this mathematics and clarifies feasible GPU-budget examples. Neither version provides theorems, proofs, or additional mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: V2 adds rapid dynamic role switching, approximately 0.7 seconds, as a principal contribution for adapting to changing online workloads. The central disaggregation, memory-efficiency, and latency claims remain. Promoting IRP into the contribution list foregrounds a component already described and evaluated in v1.

C2.justification: V2 newly discusses how full reinitialization can discard ongoing work and harm SLOs, and explains role migration as a response to changing decoding demand. It also attributes stronger NPU benefits to a larger encoding share. Existing interpretations of memory limits and model-specific encoding/prefill bottlenecks largely remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds substantial NPU implementation information, including 910B3 hardware, CANN 7.6, Ascend-vLLM versions, per-stage container APIs, and resource settings. It also documents optimizer-ablation configurations and SLO selection. Existing GPU implementation details mostly move to Appendix B, while explicit A800 memory-test captions and the explanation of DistServe's shared vLLM execution engine are dropped.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed from throughput- versus latency-oriented LLM systems to multimodal serving and disaggregation. V2 adds discussion of GEAR, SnapKV, and Inf-MLLM, contrasting their scope with cloud-serving SLO requirements. Several earlier system citations are removed, and NextQA is newly cited for the added evaluation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites and condenses the introduction, related work, method explanations, results discussion, and conclusion. Implementation, optimizer details, offline experiments, and selected results move into organized appendices. The title changes from 'multimedia' to 'multimodal,' and author/header text is revised.

P2.justification: V2 adds a scheduling illustration, a memory-capacity chart, NextQA and NPU plots, and three ablation tables. The architecture diagram is redrawn with role-switching controls, while the standalone IRP illustration is removed. The original SLO figure is split between the main text and appendix, and retained tables and offline plots are relocated.

improvement.justification: NextQA, workload-shift controls, and NPU evaluation strengthen evidence beyond v1's synthetic GPU experiments. However, v2 narrows IRP comparisons and introduces misleading summaries: the abstract calls the throughput benefit a reduction, and Section 4.3 misassigns image-capacity gains despite unchanged Table 1 values—7× belongs to MiniCPM-V and 10× to InternVL2-26B. These reporting errors and reduced comparison coverage limit the net quality improvement.
